issues.issue: The insuring promise is to pay "the proceeds of this Policy according to the following provisions," so the promise carries no content of its own and is wholly dependent on terms defined elsewhere (§2.5 Proceeds, §4.1). A court could be asked what, if anything, this cover-page undertaking adds to or qualifies in the operative payment provisions.

The 20-day free-look runs from an event the clause leaves indeterminate ("within 20 days after you rec[eive it]") and does not say whether return is measured by mailing or by the company's receipt. The refund of "any premium you have paid" also has to be squared with §3.1's rule that no coverage exists until premium is paid.

The automatic paid-up benefit at the stated policy anniversary fixes a level death benefit on the Policy Account Value less indebtedness, which cannot be squared with §4.2's Coverage Option A/B greater-of death benefit formulas or with the Termination/Maturity Date shown in Section 1. A court would have to decide which provision governs the amount payable after the paid-up date.

The definition fixes the Beneficiary as the person "named in the original application," while §8.4 provides that if no beneficiary was named in the application the Owner is the beneficiary and allows later change. The two must be read together to determine who the Beneficiary is when the application names no one or names someone later changed.

The qualifier "while this Policy is in force and the Insured is alive" is placed so that it grammatically modifies both the death payment and the surrender payment, which is impossible for a death payment. That mislocation makes it unclear whether death proceeds are conditioned on anything beyond the Policy being in force.

"The date coverage commences" is defined by cross-reference to §7.2, but §3.1 states there is no coverage until the premium is paid and §7.2 makes the date the later of the Policy Date or payment. A court could be asked which date controls when Policy Date, delivery and payment diverge.

The Age definition is left incomplete ("the Insured's age on the birthday nearest the first..."), so the anniversary or date from which age is measured is not stated. Age drives both the §4.2 risk-percentage table and the §5.4 Cost of Insurance table, so the missing measuring date is consequential.

"Planned Periodic Premium" is used in two inconsistent senses in one definition: the amount the Owner "most recently elect[s] to pay," and the fixed amount shown in Section 1 that is the mandatory minimum for two years. Which sense applies determines the §5.10 no-lapse test and §3.2(2) computation.

This definition requires the Minimum Initial Premium to be paid "before the date this Policy is delivered," whereas §3.1 requires payment "at or before the time this Policy is delivered" and §7.2 dates coverage from payment. The two timing rules differ and a court would have to reconcile them.

The definition survives only as a fragment ("application. It is used in determining the amount ... as provided in Section 6.2"), so the term being defined and the amount it determines cannot be identified from the text. A court would have to supply the defined term from context.

The Specified Amount is defined as the amount stated in the original application, while Section 1 of the Policy separately states a Specified Amount and §6.2 permits increases and decreases. Which document controls the operative Specified Amount at a given time is left to be worked out across provisions.

The Death Benefit is defined as the amount payable "prior to any adjustment specified in Section 4," yet §4.2 is itself the provision that computes the death benefit and then adjusts it for riders and indebtedness. The definition and §4.2 are circular as to whether "Death Benefit" is the pre- or post-adjustment figure.

The statement that both options give an increased death benefit "when the difference between the Policy Account Value and the death benefit reaches a minimum size" leaves "minimum size" wholly unquantified in this provision. The reader must go to §4.2's risk-percentage table to find any content for the phrase.

The definition directs the reader to "See Section 4.3" for the Monthly Insurance Charge, but Section 4.3 is Interest on Death Proceeds; the Monthly Insurance Charge is described in §5.3. The misdirected cross-reference has to be corrected against §5.3 before the definition can be applied.

"The charge we make for providing pure insurance protection" is undefined, and it is not said whether the charge may recover anything beyond mortality risk. The phrase controls what the insurer may load into the Cost of Insurance under §5.4.
The Monthly Due Date is "the same day of each month as shown in the Policy Date," which has no application in months lacking that day. The provision supplies no fallback date for such months.

"There is no insurance coverage in effect until the payment is made" cannot be squared with §7.2, which makes the Policy effective on the later of the Policy Date or payment and contemplates a Temporary Insurance Agreement given when the application was taken. Whether interim coverage exists turns on which provision controls.

The freedom to "make premium payments at any time and in any amount you choose" is stated against §3.3, which lets the insurer refuse or return premiums to preserve tax qualification, and §3.2(4), which lets it set maximum and minimum limits. The scope of the owner's payment right emerges only from reading those provisions together.

This cumulative premium test (one-twelfth of the annual Planned Periodic Premium times elapsed months) is stated differently from the first-two-year no-lapse test in §5.10, which applies the same formula but subtracts Partial Withdrawals and Policy Indebtedness. A court would have to decide whether the two tests are the same requirement or two different ones.

The insurer may change the Minimum Premium Remittance "at any time" on mere notice, which sits against §6.4's requirement that any change to the Policy not provided for be approved and signed by an officer and endorsed on the Policy. Whether a unilateral change to a Section 1 figure is effective without endorsement is unresolved.

The closing sentence ("This will happen only if payment ... would ... increase the difference between the death benefit and the Policy Account Value") leaves the referent of "This" ambiguous as between the limits, the evidence-of-insurability requirement, or both. The condition also states the opposite of what the corridor logic would suggest, so its operation is unclear.

The premium limit is tied to statutory references — TEFRA of 1982 and "Section 101F of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954" — that are misdescribed and long superseded, with only "any future applicable regulations" as a catch-all. What tax standard now governs the limit is left to construction.

The reinstatement condition requires premium sufficient for "the next two (2) Monthly Insurance Charges described in Section 5.2," but §5.2 is the Interest Rate provision; Monthly Insurance Charges are described in §5.3. The mistaken cross-reference must be resolved against §5.3 to apply the condition.

Reinstatement uses the Policy Account Value, Indebtedness and Surrender Charges "in effect when the Policy lapsed," which cannot easily be squared with §3.4(2)'s requirement of new premium and §5.2's crediting of interest for the intervening period. Whether charges and interest accrue over the lapse interval is not addressed.

The reinstatement effective date is left unstated ("will be the Mont[hly]..."), so the date from which coverage and charges resume cannot be determined from the provision. That date governs how many Monthly Insurance Charges are owed on reinstatement.

"We will pay the Surrender Value to you if the Insured is living and this Policy is in force" reads as an unconditional obligation, while §5.8 requires a surrender and §5.8's postponement clause allows payment to be deferred up to six months after written request. The trigger and timing of the surrender payment differ between the two.

"To the extent permitted by law" leaves the spendthrift protection's scope entirely to outside law without identifying which state's law applies. The Policy elsewhere refers variously to the state of delivery (§5.11) and the state of the Insured's residence (§4.3).

The amount payable is said to depend on the Coverage Option "currently in effect ... shown in Section 1," but §6.3 allows the Coverage Option to be changed after issue without amending Section 1's printed entry. Which record establishes the operative Coverage Option is unresolved.

Option A already increases the death benefit by "any premiums received since the prior Monthly Due Date" with interest, while the closing paragraph of §4.2 separately increases death benefits "by any premiums received after the date of death." The two additions overlap and a court would have to decide whether a premium can be counted twice.

Option B's corridor clause is internally garbled — "the Monthly Due Date prior to our coinciding with [the] date of death" — so the measuring date for the Policy Account Value multiplier is not clearly stated. The same sentence uses two different formulations of that date.

The increase for "any premiums received after the date of death" cannot be squared with Coverage Option A's own increase for premiums received since the prior Monthly Due Date in §4.2. Read together they may add the same premium to the death benefit twice.

Death benefits are decreased here by indebtedness, while §9.4 provides that outstanding Policy Indebtedness "will be deducted from the Policy Proceeds" — a different deduction base at a different stage. Whether indebtedness is subtracted once from the benefit or again from the proceeds is left open.

The insurer's power to modify death benefits for tax compliance sits against §6.4, which requires any change to the Policy to be approved and signed by an officer and endorsed on it, and §7.1's entire-contract clause. The provision also does not say what happens to the Policy's tax status if the Owner exercises the stated right of refusal.

Interest on death proceeds is floored by "the rate required by the state in which the Insured resides," whereas §5.6 and §5.11 measure minimum values by the law of the state in which the Policy is delivered. A court would have to decide which state's law supplies the governing minimum when the two differ.

The Policy Account Value formula "A + B + C - D - E" is stated without a legible identification of each component, and it directs the reader to "Section 2" for the Monthly Insurance Charge when that charge is described in §5.3. The account value that drives lapse, surrender and death benefit therefore cannot be computed from the provision's own words.

The worked example is arithmetically self-contradictory: "the Policy Loan Interest Rate ... less two (2) percentage points (e.g. 6% less 2 points equals 6%)." The illustration negates the rule it is meant to illustrate, leaving the rate credited on loaned account value in doubt.

The Cost of Insurance is computed "on any Premium Due Date," a term that is defined nowhere in the Policy, which elsewhere uses only "Monthly Due Date" (§2.17, §5.3). The formula's "A x (B - C)" also leaves component C unidentified in the text.

Current Cost of Insurance rates are said to be "based on the Insured's sex, current age, and risk class" and set on "our expectation of future experience," raising whether the enumerated factors are exclusive or whether other loads may be charged. That list-versus-discretion tension is the operative ambiguity in the rate-setting power.

The risk-class adjustment mechanics are unintelligible as written: clauses (a) and (b) are stated without their operative instructions ("For a flat ... rating percentage; or ... multiply the maximum cost of ..."). How a flat extra or percentage rating adjusts the guaranteed maximum rate cannot be determined from the text.

The cost of rider benefits is fixed only by reference to Section 1, whose specification page states rider charges that are not legible or complete on the face of the Policy. The charge deducted under §5.3 for the Waiver of Deduction rider therefore rests on an external table the provision does not reproduce.

The Cash Value is "equal to:" A, B and C, but no operators are given, so whether the Surrender Fee and the interest differential are subtracted or otherwise applied cannot be read from the provision. The trailing floor clause ("never be less than the minimum Cash Value required by the state in which this Policy is delivered") also stands unattached to any sentence.

The right to surrender "at any time" sits against §8.1, which conditions the Owner's exercise of Policy rights on there being no irrevocable beneficiary and no assignment, and §8.3, which subjects the Owner's rights to an assignment. Whether an assigned Policy can still be surrendered by the Owner is left to be reconciled.

The six-month postponement right cannot be squared with §4.1's flat undertaking to "pay the Surrender Value to you if the Insured is living and this Policy is in force." Nothing states which provision governs the timing of payment.

The provision allows withdrawal of part of the Cash Value "at any time" while in the same breath permitting "only two (2) withdrawals ... during any Policy year," and the ceiling ("no more than the Surrender Value less $25 and less the next Monthly Insurance Charges") is stated in fragments. The permitted amount and frequency are therefore both in doubt.

The Withdrawal Charge is "A + B + $25" but component "B" is never identified (only "...ed rate multiplied by the Partial Withdrawal" survives), so the charge cannot be computed. The following sentence's recalculation of the first-year Surrender Fee compounds the indeterminacy.

Under Option A the Specified Amount is reduced by the withdrawal and charge and "must be at least the Minimum Specified Amount," but the provision does not say what happens to a requested withdrawal that would breach that floor. Whether such a request is void, reduced, or treated as a surrender is unaddressed.
